item.title: HEP-Ex-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Performance in High Energy Physics Experiment Data Analyses with Sealed Worlds
item.description: arXiv:2611.28194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows. We demonstrate the approach on four tasks built from CMS open data and present it as a way to reliably benchmark scientific work in experimental high-energy physics. At the time of writing, the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 60% of the score of the expert reference analyses on average, ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 38% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 31%. In individual sessions on one of the tasks, Gemini 4 Argon exceeds the reference. The benchmark is hosted at https://hep-ex-bench.github.io
item.dc:creator: Andrzej Nov\'ak, Yiyang Zhao, Dolores Garcia, Eric A. Moreno, Jeffrey Krupa, V\'ictor Bres\'o-Pla, Samuel Bright-Thonney, Lukas Heinrich, Michael Kagan, Philip Harris

item.title: A Transformer-based Method for Neutrino Event Generator Reweighting
item.description: arXiv:2611.28199v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to test the effects of different neutrino event generators on simulation-based analyses is currently bottlenecked by the computational cost of propagating simulated events through expensive detector simulations. One way to circumvent this limitation is to reweight events produced with one generator to replicate the predictions of another. However, existing methods for doing this in neutrino physics tend to be limited to only a few observables at a time. We present a transformer-based architecture that can reweight between neutrino event generators based on nearly the entire particle stack, providing reweighted events that are valid over a greatly expanded phase space. We present results with events generated from multiple GENIE configurations and NuWro as examples, and we introduce an energy distance-based metric for evaluating the results in a multidimensional, unbinned manner. Our results show promising performance for realistic applications and provide a method for comparing the performance of different reweighting techniques.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Cudd, Roger G. Huang, Benjamin Nachman, Vinicius Mikuni, Callum Wilkinson

item.title: Neural-network-powered new-physics searches by predictive goodness of fit
item.description: arXiv:2611.28414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model-independent searches for new physics test whether data agree with a Reference model with unknown nuisance parameters. Because the shape and location of a signal are not specified, these tests call for flexible learners (fitting procedures such as neural networks), and a likelihood ratio maximized over a neural network falls outside the standard asymptotic theory, making the calibration a major challenge. We propose a predictive alternative: the departure from the Reference is fitted on part of the data and its likelihood gain over the fitted Reference is evaluated on the rest, cross-fitted over several folds to preserve sample efficiency. The nuisance estimation error is propagated into the variance of the test statistic to first order, in the spirit of Neyman's C(alpha) test, so that the test need not be recalibrated at each nuisance value. The randomness in the fitted departure is treated by a central limit theorem for cross-validated statistics under algorithmic stability, plus a variance correction when stability is not achieved. The calibration is analytic, and no pseudo-experiments are needed. On established one-dimensional and five-dimensional (dilepton) benchmarks, the false-positive rate always stays within Monte Carlo error of nominal across different nuisances and the learners' tuning. The test's power relative to existing learned tests is mixed: higher for some signals and lower for others, depending on how well the fitted departure captures the signal.
item.dc:creator: Jing Lei

item.title: Towards Automatic Ion Identification in Storage Rings
item.description: arXiv:2611.28070v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Resonant Schottky detectors provide non-destructive, single-ion-sensitive measurements of revolution frequencies and intensities of ion species stored in a heavy-ion storage ring. These high-\(Q\) cavities allow analysis of high-order harmonics of the revolution frequencies to magnify absolute frequency separations. Adjacent harmonic ranges can, however, overlap within the detector band, making frequency alone insufficient for determining the ion's mass-to-charge ratio $(m/q)$. We present a proof-of-concept for an automated harmonic de-overlapping method using spectral shapes in combined Schottky and Isochronous Mass Spectrometry. The empirical ansatz is that, for a fixed ion-optical setting, each peak, corresponding to a specific ion species with given $m/q$ ratio, has a characteristic profile that evolves smoothly with changing $m/q$. Occurrences of the same local structure at different harmonics should therefore retain almost identical shapes after frequency rescaling. Applied to a 245\,MHz spectrum accumulated from 11\,452 injections at the Experimental Storage Ring at GSI, the method organizes 16 of 32 detected structures into five candidate families and reconstructs their fundamental-frequency representation. Reducing the complex mixed-harmonic spectrum to this smaller candidate set solves the challenging task of finding initial anchors for the ion identification.
item.dc:creator: Anna Jule He{\ss}, David Freire-Fern\'andez, Moritz Porstend\"orfer, Wolfram Korten, Yury A. Litvinov

item.title: On the distribution function for cross-correlation estimators in cosmology and beyond
item.description: arXiv:2611.28218v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The ubiquitous Gaussian distribution, $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, has mean of zero and variance of 1. It is well known that the estimator $\widehat{x^2} = N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^2$ for the variance obtained from $N$ samples $x_i$ is drawn from a $\chi_n^2$ distribution, a result used often to assess the implications of data for a model. One often also needs to measure the covariance, or cross-correlation, of two different variables $x$ and $y$. If the distributions for $x$ and $y$ are both gaussian but independent of each other, the estimator $N^{-1}\sum_i x_i y_i$ for the cross-correlation is distributed about its expectation value (zero) with variance unity. The distribution function for this estimator may also be required to interpret data, for example in the measurement of cosmological cross-correlations. This distribution---the cross-correlation analog of the $\chi_n^2$ distribution---appears in the literature, but it has not been widely internalized by many in the field. We therefore here present two pedagogical derivations of this distribution and discuss some of its properties. We discuss in particular the connection to cosmological observables, but note several other areas of physics where these results may apply.
item.dc:creator: Robert N. Cahn, Marc Kamionkowski

item.title: Is the learner or the summary the limit? Auditing machine-learning energy reconstruction for air-shower arrays on KASCADE and GRAPES-3
item.description: arXiv:2611.29363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine-learning energy estimators for cosmic-ray arrays are usually trained on a few fitted shower parameters, not station signals. When their resolution stops improving, standard diagnostics cannot say whether a better model would help or the summary has run out of information. We use a five-step audit that compares trained models with a learner-independent estimate of the lowest error the summary allows (its squared-loss Bayes risk, or floor), tests which inputs add information and flags inputs merely computed from the fit. We apply it to public KASCADE simulations with three hadronic-interaction models (QGSJET-II-04, EPOS-LHC and SIBYLL-2.3d), to 13,848,509 measured KASCADE events and to simulated GRAPES-3 events. Within known energy decades below 10^16 eV, gradient boosting on nine reconstructed features is within 2.2% of the estimated floor under every estimator setting, so more capacity is not expected to gain more than about 2%. The floor is an estimate, accurate to about 1% in a semi-synthetic benchmark with intervals that under-cover, and not a bound on the true Bayes risk. Replacing reconstructed by true particle numbers removes 70 to 72% of the error variance below 10^15 eV and 24 to 26% between 10^16 and 10^17 eV on all three models, yet simulated station signals close about a tenth of that gap. On GRAPES-3, networks given images rendered from the fit do no better than the fit. In measured data, the mean muon size at fixed electron size lies within every model's proton-to-iron bracket and a label-free probe finds the muon channel used as in simulation; neither fixes the energy scale. Energy-labelled results are simulated.
item.dc:creator: Mugdha Raje Ashiya, Samarjeet Malik

item.title: Asymmetrical transport distribution function: skewness as a key to enhance thermoelectric performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.30565v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How to achieve high thermoelectric figure of merit is still a scientific challenge. By solving the Boltzmann transport equation, thermoelectric properties can be written as integrals of a single function, the transport distribution function (TDF). In this work, the shape effects of transport distribution function in various typical functional forms on thermoelectric properties of materials are systematically investigated. It is found that the asymmetry of TDF, characterized by skewness, can be used to describe universally the trend of thermoelectric properties. By defining symmetric and asymmetric TDF functions, a novel skewness is then constructed for thermoelectric applications. It is demonstrated, by comparison with ab initio calculations and experiments, that the proposed thermoelectric skewness not only perfectly captures the main feature of conventional skewness, but also is able to predict the thermoelectric power accurately. This comparison confirms the unique feature of our proposed thermoelectric skewness, as well as its special role of connection between the statistics of TDF and thermoelectric properties of materials. It is also found that the thermoelectric performance can be enhanced by increasing the asymmetry of TDF. Finally, it is also interesting to find that the thermoelectric transport properties based on typical quantum statistics (Fermi-Dirac distributions), can be well described by typical shape parameter (skewness) for classical statistics.
item.dc:creator: Jin-Cheng Zheng

item.title: Quantifying Errors in Chemical Kinetics
item.description: arXiv:2611.30921v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The physical structure of kinetic measurements determines the correct statistical framework for quantifying their uncertainties, yet this framework has never been explicitly derived or systematically applied in the chemical kinetics literature. Here, we derive a forward model for kinetic observations from a minimal set of stated assumptions about the measurement process, and identify the correct statistical treatment for each kinetic parameter as an explicit consequence of that model. We then audit the literature pertaining to a well-studied reaction, examining the kinetics of permanganate oxidation, to establish the scale of deviation from the correct framework. We find that of 330 measurements, 35.8% carry no uncertainty quantification of any kind and none are accompanied by a full propagation of all uncertainties. To demonstrate the practical consequences of departing from the correct framework, we reanalyse a representative kinetic dataset, first checking whether the data are consistent with the forward model and then applying the correct procedures. We find that the impacts are modest for the dataset examined, as expected for quantities determined in a low-uncertainty regime, but that uncertainties in activation energy are systematically underestimated when observed rather than assumed measurement precision is used as the basis for regression weights. We highlight that these consequences become substantially more significant at the limits of current experimental methodologies, where measurement uncertainty is large and the correct distributional treatment can no longer be approximated by standard approaches. Based on this, we propose a set of minimum recommendations for error reporting in chemical kinetics that follow directly from our forward model.
item.dc:creator: Skyla B. White, Paul B. Rimmer, Miles Cramner, Alex T. Archibald

item.title: Simple design of adaptive protocols for quantum metrology with limited data
item.description: arXiv:2611.31230v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent sensing experiments have used a Bayesian notion of precision gain to adapt control parameters for fixed measurements. Here, we advocate a simple design principle based on Personick's minimum mean square loss formalism to extend this procedure in order to include measurement optimisation, determining the optimal measurement for each probe and providing a prior-dependent precision gain to optimise the probe itself. This offers a Bayesian counterpart to protocol design based on the Fisher information, with a similar algebraic structure but incorporating the full prior. We apply this principle to adaptive phase estimation with single-mode Gaussian probes, showing that joint optimisation outperforms both adaptive homodyne detection and a fixed-probe strategy optimised for the initial prior, with a maximum reduction of 32% in mean posterior variance relative to homodyne detection. Our results illustrate the potential of simple Bayesian design for quantum metrology with limited data when measurement bases can be controlled.
item.dc:creator: Ricard Ravell Rodr\'iguez, Jes\'us Rubio

item.title: Wavescan: Multiresolution Time-Frequency Transform of Gravitational-Wave Data
item.description: arXiv:2201.01096v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Identifying transient signals embedded in non-stationary noise requires analyzing the time-dependent spectral components of the observed time series. The time-frequency distribution of the signal power can be estimated with Gabor atoms, or wavelets, localized in time and frequency by a window function. Such analysis is constrained by the Heisenberg-Gabor uncertainty principle, which limits the simultaneous time and frequency localization achievable with individual wavelets. Moreover, the resulting time-frequency distribution is subject to temporal and spectral leakage, limiting the identification of sharp or rapidly varying features in the power spectrum. This paper introduces a time-frequency transform that uses a stack of wavelets to scan local power across multiple scales. At each time-frequency location, a wavelet least affected by the leakage is selected from the stack to obtain high-resolution localization of power. The resulting wavelet scan ("wavescan") extends conventional multiresolution analysis by enhancing time-frequency localization and mitigating local power distortions caused by temporal and spectral leakage. The paper describes the principal components of the wavescan framework, including the estimation of the time-varying spectrum, identification of transient signals in the time-frequency data, and reconstruction of the corresponding time-domain waveforms. To demonstrate the performance of the method, the wavescan transform is applied to gravitational-wave data from the LIGO detectors.
item.dc:creator: Sergey Klimenko

item.title: Wavelet-domain flow-matching posterior estimation for LISA signals with data gaps
item.description: arXiv:2512.18290v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) data stream will contain scheduled and unscheduled gaps, which break the stationarity of the instrumental noise and invalidate the standard frequency-domain likelihood. Amortized simulation-based inference (SBI) avoids explicit likelihood evaluations, but its application to months-long observations requires compressing high-dimensional, gapped time series while preserving information about source parameters. We develop an end-to-end amortized posterior estimation pipeline: the gapped data are mapped to noise-scaled Wilson-Daubechies-Meyer (WDM) wavelet coefficients and summarized by a convolutional-Transformer network, trained jointly with a flow-matching (FM) posterior estimator, with optional importance-sampling correction. For a LISA-like signal observed for 3 months, the amortized FM posteriors are well calibrated on simulated observations whose waveforms and gaps were not seen in training. The FM posteriors agree closely with the benchmark, the posteriors from parallel-tempered Markov chain Monte Carlo (PTMCMC), although they exhibit moderately greater dispersion. Importance sampling efficiently reweights the FM posterior, achieving close agreement with the benchmark at modest additional cost.
item.dc:creator: Ruiting Mao, Jeong Eun Lee, Matthew C. Edwards

item.title: Structural and Lagrangian properties of analogue ensembles to characterize multifractality of stochastic processes
item.description: arXiv:2605.08155v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a framework for the scale-invariance characterization of stochastic processes in reconstructed finite-dimensional spaces. This framework analyses the structural and dynamical properties of the reconstructed space and is based on a Takens embedding reconstruction followed by the definition of ensembles of analogue states. First, we specify a collection of target states densely sampling the full embedding space. For each target state, we search for the ensemble of its k-nearest neighbors, its k-best analogues, and we analyze its volume and dynamics. On the one hand, we study the probability distribution of the volumes and relate its mean and variance to the scale-invariance properties of the stochastic process. On the second hand, we study the Lagrangian properties of the analogues by characterizing how they disperse in time. More particularly, we study the volume occupied by the analogue's successors in function of time and of their initial volume. The main contribution of this paper is to highlight the link between these dynamical properties and the scale-invariance features of the process. We analyze two types of stationary and dissipative 1-dimensional scale-invariant processes: regularized fractional Brownian motion and regularized multifractal random walk. For both processes, the structure and dynamics of the embedding space are determined by their scale-invariant properties.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Granero-Belinchon (ODYSSEY, IMT Atlantique - MEE, Lab-STICC\_OSE)

item.title: Growing Hypergraphs with Homophily
item.description: arXiv:2607.16046v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: There are many extant models of hypergraphs with interactions governed by attribute-based homophily between nodes, but most assume independence between edges conditional on node parameters. Relaxing this assumption, we study a mechanistic model of growing hypergraphs in which edge formation is influenced by both previous edges and binary node labels. Edges form in this model as noisy copies of previous edges, where the transmission of nodes from one edge to the next depends on multiple homophilic mechanisms between labels. These homophilic mechanisms give rise to tunable assortative structure in the hypergraph. We derive a power law for the degree distribution in this model and describe the long-term dynamics of the joint distribution of labels contained in edges. Our model defines a likelihood over a labeled hypergraph, allowing us to use standard maximum-likelihood techniques to structure algorithms. We estimate the model parameters on synthetic and real data via (stochastic) expectation maximization. These estimates give statistically-principled descriptions of the operation of homophily in empirical polyadic systems. We also demonstrate an approach to community detection via simulated annealing which, though computationally expensive, achieves competitive results on both synthetic data and certain empirical data sets known to be challenging to community detection techniques based on the edge-independence assumption. Our findings highlight the benefits of incorporating edge- and label-dependence in higher-order modeling and data analysis, and point to several directions for future work.
item.dc:creator: Violet Ross, Francis Cataldo, Philip S. Chodrow

item.title: Probabilistic framework for infrastructure deformation anomaly warning using InSAR observations
item.description: arXiv:2610.13552v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) offers a low-cost, wide-area solution for near continuous infrastructure monitoring. However, translating InSAR observations into automated anomaly warnings remains challenging because displacements are relative, affected by uncertainty, and acquired along line of sight (LOS). This paper introduces a probabilistic warning framework that accounts for these factors. LOS displacements are modelled through a Gaussian distribution. A limit state function is defined to describe the displacement exceedance, and the time-dependent probability of exceedance is evaluated. Instead of a fixed threshold, warnings are identified through abrupt increases in exceedance probability. The framework is tested using three case studies of quay walls in Amsterdam, The Netherlands, providing timely anomaly warnings and issued no warnings for the non-collapse case. Results demonstrate the potential of a probabilistic interpretation of InSAR time series for deformation anomaly warning.
item.dc:creator: Hao Kuai, Na Hao, Pantelis Karamitopoulos, Alice Cicirello, Giorgia Giardina

item.title: Deglobalising the fit: how to search for physics beyond vacuum General Relativity in LISA catalogues
item.description: arXiv:2610.27069v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna will observe up to $\sim 10^{7}$ overlapping signals, which have to be characterised simultaneously with a \emph{global} fit. This is a challenge for model comparison since rerunning the global fit for every model of interest, including deviations from vacuum General Relativity, is computationally demanding. An alternative is a two-step post-processing strategy: a first global fit with vacuum models only, after which selected target sources are reanalysed under a different model with all other sources subtracted. We show that in this strategy a beyond-vacuum effect in a target source can be partly absorbed by the overlapping \textit{nuisance} sources in the first fit, subtracted with them, and never reach the reanalysis. In the linear-signal approximation, the loss in reported detection significance is captured by a single number, the \emph{masking ratio} $\mathcal{R}\in[0,1]$: a deviation the global fit would detect at $n_\sigma$ is reported by post-processing at $\mathcal{R}\,n_\sigma$, and, for a single beyond-vacuum parameter, bounds in null tests are reported too tight by the same factor. We show how to compute $\mathcal{R}$ from the posterior samples of the vacuum global fit, and give an algorithm that ranks the nuisance sources by how much of the effect each can absorb, so that only the most correlated ones need to be refitted with the target. We validate our method with full Markov-chain Monte Carlo inference on a toy model of 21 overlapping chirping sinusoids, one of which carries a small non-linear chirp that represents the missed physics. Using our post-processing recipe, we are able to recover the global-fit result on the beyond-vacuum parameter to within $0.15\sigma$ by refitting only 4 of the 20 nuisance sources. This method can serve as a basis for tests of General Relativity in realistic LISA mock datasets.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Duque, Jonathan Gair
